# Historical Development of African Art Music: From Oral Transmission and Cosmopolitan Exchange to Contemporary Intercultural Composition

## Framing “African Art Music”
African art music denotes concert music (“fine art music”) distinguished by crafted form, expressive intent, and aesthetic refinement, while being rooted in African musical traditions, aesthetics, and cultural discourse rather than in entertainment markets alone.<cite id="9b98a368-1">The term art music or fine art music is used for music designed for intent listening or concert presentation, combining expressive feeling with high craftsmanship; African art music refers to works that manifest these attributes and are rooted in African traditions</cite> <cite id="9b98a368-0">Contemporary African art music builds on progenitors through blending indigenous idioms with Western structures, engaging creative ethnomusicology, social commentary, and Yoruba cultural values</cite>. In practice, African composers have long fused African and Western resources, with interculturalism characterizing much of twentieth- and twenty-first-century practice across choral, art-song, and instrumental spheres.<cite id="0d192ade-0">Interculturalism is part of twentieth-century African experience, with neo-African art music ranging from predominantly Western idiom to predominantly African idioms, and popular genres like Highlife, Jazz, Rumba, Juju, Kwela, Pachanga, and Mbalax themselves being intercultural</cite> <cite id="0d192ade-1">Ghanaian choral and instrumental art music often merge traditional rhythms and folk motifs with scholarly techniques, exemplified by the Sankɔfa Symphony’s Apatampa-based movement</cite>.

## Precolonial Aesthetics and Oral Compositionality
Across sub-Saharan Africa, precolonial music was organized around rhythmic complexity, polyphony/polyrhythm, conversational interaction, and improvisational development, often tied to social, ritual, and political life rather than to written notation.<cite id="0d192ade-3">Precolonial African music emphasized rhythm over melody/harmony, used repetition as an organizing principle, relied on improvisation, and was frequently group-based with polyphony, polyrhythm, and a conversational style</cite>. Ethnographic accounts stress that traditional music existed largely outside literacy and formal criticism, with knowledge transmitted orally and situated in performance practice and communal meaning-making.<cite id="9b98a368-3">African traditional music largely escaped literacy and institutions like art criticism; local forms and structures (rhythmic patterns, motives, cadences) guided composition and performance, with social-historical changes driving stylistic change</cite>. These precolonial resources—rhythmic prototypes, melodic motifs, and cadential formulas—became the raw materials that later composers drew upon to articulate new concert repertories.<cite id="9b98a368-2">Composers inherit fixed forms and structures—rhythmic patterns, melodic motives, cadential patterns—and draw upon them to make new musical statements, enabling authentic identity while exploring creativity beyond event-specific constraints</cite>.

## Colonial Contact, Ethnomusicological Framing, and Racialized Hierarchies
European contact disrupted and reconfigured African musical life, catalyzing hybrid genres and new classificatory regimes. Colonial ethnography foregrounded “traditional” sources and musical elements, laying groundwork for later nation-building projects and concert-music appropriation of these categories.<cite id="9b98a368-4">ILAM’s early African Music journal emphasized ethnographic description of African musical groups and elements (pitch, harmony, rhythm, form), transcriptions, and theory, reflecting limited engagement with African Studies discourses on decolonization</cite>. At the same time, colonial and apartheid-era hierarchies seeped into aesthetic valuation: “art music” was sometimes used to privilege university-trained, Eurocentric compositional models over vernacular and self-taught Black practices, functioning as a marker of intellectual and social superiority.<cite id="a58c079f-3">In South Africa, ‘art music’ distinguished university-educated Black and white composers’ work from that of Black composers without university access, implicitly marking the latter’s music as inferior; the author rejects ‘art music’ as a discriminatory term and prefers ‘contemporary music’</cite>. These hierarchies intersected with global modernist canons, as Euro-American modernism selectively valorized certain African sounds while marginalizing others, a dynamic that contemporary African composers confront and negotiate.<cite id="0d192ade-4">Popular music is imagined as socially embedded and accessible, while ‘Darmstadt/Newe Musik’ carries an aura of elite serialism; such dichotomies reproduce class and cultural hierarchies that African composers must navigate</cite>.

## Early Nationalist Projects and State-Mediated Modernism
Post-independence, many African states embraced music as a vehicle for nation-building, identity articulation, and political mobilization, supporting institutions and repertories that could symbolize unity and modernity.<cite id="a58c079f-1">In Zambia, from pre-independence resistance to post-independence nation-building under UNIP, music (e.g., akalela, Chitwansombo) fostered unity, promoted African Humanism and patriotism, and later reflected dissent and societal struggles</cite>. In South Africa, missionary and school systems seeded choral traditions that became crucial sites for vernacular expression and cultural preservation, later amplified by post-apartheid composers who fused Western techniques with indigenous styles.<cite id="a58c079f-4">Missionary settlers established African choral music, and contemporary South African choral composers combine Western and African idioms; a collective effort among academics, policymakers, and universities sustains indigenous choral identity</cite>. These national projects helped normalize concert practices while drawing on African resources—rhythms, modes, and community-based aesthetics—to craft “national” or “authentic” soundscapes that could address both local audiences and global listeners.<cite id="9b98a368-1">Composers reconcile Western techniques with African resources, treating popular and traditional vernaculars with reverence to create works that manifest craftsmanship and beauty rooted in African traditions</cite>.

## Transnational Popular Genres as Catalysts: Highlife, Afrobeat, and Beyond
Twentieth-century transnational genres—most notably Highlife—bridged popular and concert practices, normalizing orchestral instruments and danceable hybrids that later informed symphonic and chamber works.<cite id="0d192ade-0">Highlife is a twentieth-century African experience and an intercultural synthesis, with neo-African art music categories spanning Western idioms with varying African references; orchestral and choral scholarly compositions draw on these intercultural practices</cite>. In West Africa and beyond, these genres synthesized traditional rhythms, European harmony, and colonial urban textures, later inspiring composers to orchestrate traditional materials and folk themes with classical structures.<cite id="9b98a368-2">Drawing on established traditional rhythmic and melodic structures allows composers to transcend event-specific constraints, enabling performance in varied settings and fostering identity and creativity</cite>. By the late twentieth century, Afrobeat and related rhythms became global signifiers of African modernity, reinforcing the link between popular and concert aesthetics and providing repertoires that postcolonial states and diasporic artists adapted for political expression and international visibility.<cite id="a58c079f-0">Indigenous South African music’s resurgence affirmed cultural identity and heritage while serving as a tool for political articulation; global resonance of Afrobeat and traditional rhythms positioned African artists as cultural ambassadors</cite> <cite id="a58c079f-1">Political songs and national symbols in Zambia exemplify how popular and state-endorsed repertories articulate unity and leadership, with music beyond entertainment fostering shared identity</cite>.

## The Contemporary Intercultural Turn: “Afro-Classical” and Orchestral Infrastructures
Since the 1990s, a new generation of composers has expanded orchestral and choral writing, explicitly fusing African idioms with contemporary Western techniques in what scholars describe as “Afro-classical” or cross-cultural art-music practice.<cite id="0d192ade-1">Ghanaian scholarship and composition foreground interculturalism, exemplified by the Sankɔfa Symphony’s movement that merges Apatampa rhythms and folk motifs with scholarly orchestration</cite> <cite id="a58c079f-2">Interculturalism shapes choral, art-song, and instrumental spheres, with Ghanaian orchestral works addressing gaps in African resource use and inspiring preservation of cultural heritage</cite>. This turn is rooted in oral and folk repositories but articulated through symphonic forms, chamber ensembles, and global publishing infrastructures, enabling African music to travel across diasporic communities and international festivals.<cite id="9b98a368-0">Contemporary African art music integrates indigenous and Western structures while offering social commentary and cultural reclamation, aided by global networks and formal training</cite>. Composers also grapple with the fraught label “art music,” which can encode colonial and class hierarchies; many now foreground community-centered and vernacular-inflected practices to decouple composition from elitist modernist lineages.<cite id="a58c079f-3">‘Art music’ can function as a marker of social and political discrimination in South Africa; adopting ‘contemporary music’ resists classed hierarchies linking elite serialism with moral authority</cite>.

## Method, Media, and Global Markets
As African art music has globalized, debates have shifted from “authenticity” to infrastructural access, education, and market mediation. Ethnographic practice-based research and creative scholarship help document hybrid processes while building repertoires that can be taught, recorded, and disseminated.<cite id="9b98a368-2">Exploring African musical resources for composition is part of an ongoing cultural process that blends Western practice with traditional forms, expanding expressive modes and enabling performance beyond event-specific constraints</cite>. Orchestral writing has grown more prominent, though unevenly, with persistent deficits in orchestral training and commissions outside certain countries and diasporas; this asymmetry fuels new frameworks that pair local resources with global orchestral idioms.<cite id="0d192ade-1">Orchestral art music in Ghana appears historically underexploited relative to choral and popular spheres, creating a gap that contemporary works like ‘Kwesi Gyan’ aim to fill through practice-based research and preservation</cite>. Digital platforms and festival circuits now accelerate circulation, enabling African composers to reach audiences who might otherwise overlook concert music rooted in vernacular traditions.<cite id="a58c079f-0">Global resonance of indigenous genres like Afrobeat demonstrates how African music can function as cultural ambassadors, connecting communities to international audiences and supporting the African Renaissance</cite>.

## Synthesis: A Recursive History of Hybridity and Decolonization
The trajectory of African art music is best understood as recursive: precolonial oral compositionality supplied rhythmic and modal materials; colonial contact and ethnography framed these as “traditional” and seeded national and popular hybrids; postcolonial states and intellectuals mobilized music for identity and politics; transnational genres like Highlife and Afrobeat normalized orchestral and dance-based aesthetics; and contemporary composers orchestrate these cross-cultural resources into concert repertories while decolonizing categories and institutions.<cite id="9b98a368-3">Social-historical events—colonialism and globalization—reshape styles, yet African music maintains ‘simultaneous multidimensionality’ and polysemic performance</cite> <cite id="0d192ade-0">Interculturalism spans popular and art music, with neo-African art music categories reflecting diverse fusions from Highlife to Mbalax</cite> <cite id="a58c079f-3">Reframing ‘contemporary music’ counters hierarchies that privilege elite modernist lineages and marginalize vernacular and popular practices</cite>. Looking ahead, the field’s growth depends on expanding orchestral education and infrastructure, diversifying publishing and performance networks, and sustaining ethnographic-creative research that links community knowledge systems to concert-hall practice.<cite id="9b98a368-0">Research-based compositions that blend indigenous elements with formal training are seen as vital for authenticity and innovation in contemporary African art music</cite> <cite id="0d192ade-1">Practice-based research and cross-cultural frameworks can inspire preservation and creative development of African musical arts within orchestral forms</cite>.

## Notes on Scope and Gaps
This synthesis draws on ethnomusicological and compositional scholarship that emphasizes hybridity, postcolonial critique, and intercultural method. While it highlights key periods and case studies (oral transmission; Highlife/Afrobeat; South African and Ghanaian national projects; contemporary orchestral fusion), it does not exhaust institutions like Ghana’s IRMA or detailed debates on Meyer/Béhague’s typologies; those require targeted institutional histories and musicological casebooks. Nonetheless, the cited studies provide convergent evidence on the historical mechanisms—oral inheritance, transnational exchange, state patronage, and contemporary decolonial composition—that have shaped African art music’s development.<cite id="9b98a368-4">ILAM’s long-running role documents shifts from formalistic description to engagement with African Studies discourses on decolonization</cite> <cite id="0d192ade-0">A typology of neo-African art music underscores the spectrum of intercultural fusions across genres and ensembles</cite>.

# Historical Development of African Art Music: From Oral Transmission and Cosmopolitan Exchange to Contemporary Intercultural Composition

## Framing “African Art Music”
African art music denotes concert music (“fine art music”) distinguished by crafted form, expressive intent, and aesthetic refinement, while being rooted in African musical traditions, aesthetics, and cultural discourse rather than in entertainment markets alone.<cite id="9b98a368-1">The term art music or fine art music is used for music designed for intent listening or concert presentation, combining expressive feeling with high craftsmanship; African art music refers to works that manifest these attributes and are rooted in African traditions</cite> <cite id="9b98a368-0">Contemporary African art music builds on progenitors through blending indigenous idioms with Western structures, engaging creative ethnomusicology, social commentary, and Yoruba cultural values</cite>. In practice, African composers have long fused African and Western resources, with interculturalism characterizing much of twentieth- and twenty-first-century practice across choral, art-song, and instrumental spheres.<cite id="0d192ade-0">Interculturalism is part of twentieth-century African experience, with neo-African art music ranging from predominantly Western idiom to predominantly African idioms, and popular genres like Highlife, Jazz, Rumba, Juju, Kwela, Pachanga, and Mbalax themselves being intercultural</cite> <cite id="0d192ade-1">Ghanaian choral and instrumental art music often merge traditional rhythms and folk motifs with scholarly techniques, exemplified by the Sankɔfa Symphony’s Apatampa-based movement</cite>.

## Precolonial Aesthetics and Oral Compositionality
Across sub-Saharan Africa, precolonial music was organized around rhythmic complexity, polyphony/polyrhythm, conversational interaction, and improvisational development, often tied to social, ritual, and political life rather than to written notation.<cite id="0d192ade-3">Precolonial African music emphasized rhythm over melody/harmony, used repetition as an organizing principle, relied on improvisation, and was frequently group-based with polyphony, polyrhythm, and a conversational style</cite>. Ethnographic accounts stress that traditional music existed largely outside literacy and formal criticism, with knowledge transmitted orally and situated in performance practice and communal meaning-making.<cite id="9b98a368-3">African traditional music largely escaped literacy and institutions like art criticism; local forms and structures (rhythmic patterns, motives, cadences) guided composition and performance, with social-historical changes driving stylistic change</cite>. These precolonial resources—rhythmic prototypes, melodic motifs, and cadential formulas—became the raw materials that later composers drew upon to articulate new concert repertories.<cite id="9b98a368-2">Composers inherit fixed forms and structures—rhythmic patterns, melodic motives, cadential patterns—and draw upon them to make new musical statements, enabling authentic identity while exploring creativity beyond event-specific constraints</cite>.

## Colonial Contact, Ethnomusicological Framing, and Racialized Hierarchies
European contact disrupted and reconfigured African musical life, catalyzing hybrid genres and new classificatory regimes. Colonial ethnography foregrounded “traditional” sources and musical elements, laying groundwork for later nation-building projects and concert-music appropriation of these categories.<cite id="9b98a368-4">ILAM’s early African Music journal emphasized ethnographic description of African musical groups and elements (pitch, harmony, rhythm, form), transcriptions, and theory, reflecting limited engagement with African Studies discourses on decolonization</cite>. At the same time, colonial and apartheid-era hierarchies seeped into aesthetic valuation: “art music” was sometimes used to privilege university-trained, Eurocentric compositional models over vernacular and self-taught Black practices, functioning as a marker of intellectual and social superiority.<cite id="a58c079f-3">In South Africa, ‘art music’ distinguished university-educated Black and white composers’ work from that of Black composers without university access, implicitly marking the latter’s music as inferior; the author rejects ‘art music’ as a discriminatory term and prefers ‘contemporary music’</cite>. These hierarchies intersected with global modernist canons, as Euro-American modernism selectively valorized certain African sounds while marginalizing others, a dynamic that contemporary African composers confront and negotiate.<cite id="0d192ade-4">Popular music is imagined as socially embedded and accessible, while ‘Darmstadt/Newe Musik’ carries an aura of elite serialism; such dichotomies reproduce class and cultural hierarchies that African composers must navigate</cite>.

## Early Nationalist Projects and State-Mediated Modernism
Post-independence, many African states embraced music as a vehicle for nation-building, identity articulation, and political mobilization, supporting institutions and repertories that could symbolize unity and modernity.<cite id="a58c079f-1">In Zambia, from pre-independence resistance to post-independence nation-building under UNIP, music (e.g., akalela, Chitwansombo) fostered unity, promoted African Humanism and patriotism, and later reflected dissent and societal struggles</cite>. In South Africa, missionary and school systems seeded choral traditions that became crucial sites for vernacular expression and cultural preservation, later amplified by post-apartheid composers who fused Western techniques with indigenous styles.<cite id="a58c079f-4">Missionary settlers established African choral music, and contemporary South African choral composers combine Western and African idioms; a collective effort among academics, policymakers, and universities sustains indigenous choral identity</cite>. These national projects helped normalize concert practices while drawing on African resources—rhythms, modes, and community-based aesthetics—to craft “national” or “authentic” soundscapes that could address both local audiences and global listeners.<cite id="9b98a368-1">Composers reconcile Western techniques with African resources, treating popular and traditional vernaculars with reverence to create works that manifest craftsmanship and beauty rooted in African traditions</cite>.

## Transnational Popular Genres as Catalysts: Highlife, Afrobeat, and Beyond
Twentieth-century transnational genres—most notably Highlife—bridged popular and concert practices, normalizing orchestral instruments and danceable hybrids that later informed symphonic and chamber works.<cite id="0d192ade-0">Highlife is a twentieth-century African experience and an intercultural synthesis, with neo-African art music categories spanning Western idioms with varying African references; orchestral and choral scholarly compositions draw on these intercultural practices</cite>. In West Africa and beyond, these genres synthesized traditional rhythms, European harmony, and colonial urban textures, later inspiring composers to orchestrate traditional materials and folk themes with classical structures.<cite id="9b98a368-2">Drawing on established traditional rhythmic and melodic structures allows composers to transcend event-specific constraints, enabling performance in varied settings and fostering identity and creativity</cite>. By the late twentieth century, Afrobeat and related rhythms became global signifiers of African modernity, reinforcing the link between popular and concert aesthetics and providing repertoires that postcolonial states and diasporic artists adapted for political expression and international visibility.<cite id="a58c079f-0">Indigenous South African music’s resurgence affirmed cultural identity and heritage while serving as a tool for political articulation; global resonance of Afrobeat and traditional rhythms positioned African artists as cultural ambassadors</cite> <cite id="a58c079f-1">Political songs and national symbols in Zambia exemplify how popular and state-endorsed repertories articulate unity and leadership, with music beyond entertainment fostering shared identity</cite>.

## The Contemporary Intercultural Turn: “Afro-Classical” and Orchestral Infrastructures
Since the 1990s, a new generation of composers has expanded orchestral and choral writing, explicitly fusing African idioms with contemporary Western techniques in what scholars describe as “Afro-classical” or cross-cultural art-music practice.<cite id="0d192ade-1">Ghanaian scholarship and composition foreground interculturalism, exemplified by the Sankɔfa Symphony’s movement that merges Apatampa rhythms and folk motifs with scholarly orchestration</cite> <cite id="a58c079f-2">Interculturalism shapes choral, art-song, and instrumental spheres, with Ghanaian orchestral works addressing gaps in African resource use and inspiring preservation of cultural heritage</cite>. This turn is rooted in oral and folk repositories but articulated through symphonic forms, chamber ensembles, and global publishing infrastructures, enabling African music to travel across diasporic communities and international festivals.<cite id="9b98a368-0">Contemporary African art music integrates indigenous and Western structures while offering social commentary and cultural reclamation, aided by global networks and formal training</cite>. Composers also grapple with the fraught label “art music,” which can encode colonial and class hierarchies; many now foreground community-centered and vernacular-inflected practices to decouple composition from elitist modernist lineages.<cite id="a58c079f-3">‘Art music’ can function as a marker of social and political discrimination in South Africa; adopting ‘contemporary music’ resists classed hierarchies linking elite serialism with moral authority</cite>.

## Method, Media, and Global Markets
As African art music has globalized, debates have shifted from “authenticity” to infrastructural access, education, and market mediation. Ethnographic practice-based research and creative scholarship help document hybrid processes while building repertoires that can be taught, recorded, and disseminated.<cite id="9b98a368-2">Exploring African musical resources for composition is part of an ongoing cultural process that blends Western practice with traditional forms, expanding expressive modes and enabling performance beyond event-specific constraints</cite>. Orchestral writing has grown more prominent, though unevenly, with persistent deficits in orchestral training and commissions outside certain countries and diasporas; this asymmetry fuels new frameworks that pair local resources with global orchestral idioms.<cite id="0d192ade-1">Orchestral art music in Ghana appears historically underexploited relative to choral and popular spheres, creating a gap that contemporary works like ‘Kwesi Gyan’ aim to fill through practice-based research and preservation</cite>. Digital platforms and festival circuits now accelerate circulation, enabling African composers to reach audiences who might otherwise overlook concert music rooted in vernacular traditions.<cite id="a58c079f-0">Global resonance of indigenous genres like Afrobeat demonstrates how African music can function as cultural ambassadors, connecting communities to international audiences and supporting the African Renaissance</cite>.

## Synthesis: A Recursive History of Hybridity and Decolonization
The trajectory of African art music is best understood as recursive: precolonial oral compositionality supplied rhythmic and modal materials; colonial contact and ethnography framed these as “traditional” and seeded national and popular hybrids; postcolonial states and intellectuals mobilized music for identity and politics; transnational genres like Highlife and Afrobeat normalized orchestral and dance-based aesthetics; and contemporary composers orchestrate these cross-cultural resources into concert repertories while decolonizing categories and institutions.<cite id="9b98a368-3">Social-historical events—colonialism and globalization—reshape styles, yet African music maintains ‘simultaneous multidimensionality’ and polysemic performance</cite> <cite id="0d192ade-0">Interculturalism spans popular and art music, with neo-African art music categories reflecting diverse fusions from Highlife to Mbalax</cite> <cite id="a58c079f-3">Reframing ‘contemporary music’ counters hierarchies that privilege elite modernist lineages and marginalize vernacular and popular practices</cite>. ## Notes on Scope and Gaps
This synthesis draws on ethnomusicological and compositional scholarship that emphasizes hybridity, postcolonial critique, and intercultural method. While it highlights key periods and case studies (oral transmission; Highlife/Afrobeat; South African and Ghanaian national projects; contemporary orchestral fusion), it does not exhaust institutions like Ghana’s IRMA or detailed debates on Meyer/Béhague’s typologies; those require targeted institutional histories and musicological casebooks. ⮚ Composers whose works are predominantly Western in idiom with little or no reference to African elements.

⮚ Composers whose works are Western in idiom and instrumentation but borrow thematic materials from African sources.

Appropriating Akin Euba's concept of categorising neo-African art music into African popular music, it is evident that highlife music is also a twentieth-century African experience (Coffie, 2012).Therefore, the second category, which aligns with the thematic intercultural activity, is preferred when conceptualising the framework.

Title: Soundtrack of a Nation: Tracing Zambia’s Political Journey Through Music from 1960–2016
Snippet: Zambia's political and musical history is deeply intertwined, reflecting the nation's journey from colonialism to independence and its post-independence evolution (Mwila & Kalinde, 2024). During the pre-independence colonial era, music served as a vital tool for resistance and unity. Traditional songs, dances, and chants were repurposed to inspire nationalism and mobilize support for freedom movements such as the United National Independence Party (UNIP) and the African National Congress (ANC) (Masiye, 2021). Indigenous music such as akalela played a significant role in fostering solidarity across Zambia's diverse tribal groups, reinforcing a collective aspiration for independence (Namuyamba et al, 2018). 

After independence in 1964, music transitioned from a medium of resistance to a tool for nation-building. During the (UNIP) under President Kenneth Kaunda, music became a vehicle to promote African Humanism, unity, and patriotism. Songs like Tiyende pamodzi symbolised collective action, while establishing cultural institutions showcased Zambia's diversity, reinforcing a shared national identity (Lamba, 2023). The intertwining of music and politics during the UNIP reign remains a fascinating chapter in Zambia's history as music played a crucial role in shaping political consciousness, mobilising social movements, and fostering a shared national identity in Zambia. Chitwansombo songs and President Kaunda's strategic use of music was pivotal in reinforcing the nation-building process and affirming leadership. Music went beyond entertainment, becoming an essential tool for political expression and unity in the struggle for independence and post-independence efforts (Lamba, 2023;Bitter, 2023). 

During the one-party state era from 1973 to 1991, music became both propagandistic and celebratory under Kaunda's leadership (Lamba, 2023). It was used to promote loyalty to the UNIP ideology and Kaunda's humanist philosophy. However, music also served as a subtle platform for dissent, with compositions like "salaula" reflecting societal struggles and growing public discontent (Hansen, 2000). The return to multiparty democracy in 1991 brought a new role for music in Zambia's political landscape (Musiker, 2020).

I hope that sharing my experiences can offer a small window into understanding the complexities of contemporary African music today, and the various levels of creative influence imposed on African composers by the context in which they work, which is often rooted in historical race politics. 

In South Africa, the term 'art music' was introduced to distinguish music produced by university-educated Black Africans or white Africans from compositions produced by Black African composers who are either self-taught or learned composing through informal mentorship. Music written by those who composed music without studying at the university (a system to which Black composers did not have access during apartheid) was considered inferior. The term 'art music' is therefore problematic as it indirectly implies an Other music (for example, African choral music), which is of lower intellectual quality. I thus view the usage of the term 'art music' as a means of political and social discrimination against music produced by mainly Black African composers. It is for this reason that I will be using the term 'contemporary music' rather than 'art music'. The distinction in terminology is critical in understanding the class division embedded in the term. The class implication of this terminology is observed in other countries too, where this division is used alongside aesthetical preference as a descriptor of quality. 

In December 2021, I met with colleagues from Germany working in the pop music industry to discuss a possible collaboration. At one point, a colleague remarked -almost dismissively -that his and his students' approach was not like that of the 'Darmstadt crew', by which he meant the tradition of Neue Musik associated with the Darmstadt Summer Courses. His comment underscored a persistent perception: Darmstadt remains linked to the intellectual aura of serialism shaped by Karlheinz Stockhausen and Pierre Boulez, whose methodical approaches once defined its cultural authority. 18 Although the course has since diversified, the legacy of exclusivity persists, reinforcing the notion that contemporary music is the preserve of an educated elite. Below is a synthesis of how scholarly historiography distinguishes “African art music” from other African musical traditions, drawing on debates in ethnomusicology, African musicology, and case studies across West, East, and Southern Africa.

Overview: Categories and their contested status
Historiography in African music studies has long grappled with how to classify “music” across cultural contexts. Early work often framed African music through anthropological or ethnomusicological lenses that emphasized cultural totality and performance-in-context, creating tensions with musicological approaches focused on formal analysis and concert practice. Over the twentieth century, scholars such as Kwabena Nketia helped found an African musicology that claimed structural analysis and legitimacy for African music within musicological discourse, while critiques highlighted that the academy has frequently represented African music through Euro-American paradigms and that “oralism” has been used to place African traditions in a lower epistemic position. These debates set the stage for distinguishing “art music” as a concert-oriented, formally trained, and analyzable tradition, contrasted with vernacular, ritual, and popular idioms, while also cautioning against essentializing categories. <cite id="472408a0-1">Recent developments question the musicological/ethnomusicological dichotomy and argue for structural analysis of African music as a legitimate object of musicology, countering anti-formalist critiques that deny analytic legitimacy to African music</cite> <cite id="472408a0-2">Nketia and Kubik delineate a “African music” distinct from West and Orient, emphasizing shared internal patterns and contextual similarities, while also grounding distinctions in ethnographic analysis and ethnicity</cite> <cite id="472408a0-4">African musicology emerges from Nketia’s program and ILAM, positioning African musicology as a distinct mode from ethnomusicology</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-4">Decolonial critiques argue African music remains framed by Euro-American theories and oral-centric definitions, prompting calls for African-oriented theoretical and methodological tools</cite>.

Operational distinctions in historiography
Scholarly treatments converge on several operational distinctions that mark “art music” in African historiography: concert-intent and aesthetics; Western techniques and notation; institutionalized training; repertoire circulation; and audience/space.

- Concert-intent, craftsmanship, and aesthetics: Historiography commonly defines art music as music designed for “intent listening” or concert presentation, combining expressive feeling with a high level of craftsmanship and sense of beauty; when African works are described as “art music,” they are understood as manifesting these attributes and being rooted in African traditions. This definition provides an evaluative but culturally relativized template for distinguishing concert repertoire from other genres. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Art music is defined as music for “concert” presentation combining expressive intent with high craftsmanship and beauty; African art music refers to works that manifest these attributes and are rooted in African traditions</cite>.

- Western techniques and notation as infrastructures: Comparative-historic work emphasizes how Western compositional techniques and notational systems (staff and tonic solfa) became central to African “art” composition, despite indigenous complexities. Agawu’s program argues African musics can be analyzed with the same theoretical regimes used for Western art music, insisting that widely adopted staff and tonic solfa notations, though “foreign,” no longer be dismissed as inauthentic because of their entrenched use by literate and semi-literate musicians. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Nigerian and Ghanaian studies show African composers integrating Western techniques and diverse idioms, treating vernacular influences with reverence as they adopt Western practices</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-3">Agawu contends African music can be fitted to Western parameters and argues staff notation and tonic solfa, despite foreign origins, are widely used and cannot be dismissed as inauthentic</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-0">Choral practice and competition/festival contexts have promoted transcription methods (e.g., Tonic Solfa) and show Western-educated African composers reaching mass audiences, underscoring the role of written systems</cite>.

- Formal conservatory/ABC pedagogy vs oral apprenticeship: Nigerian scholarship explicitly distinguishes “art music” as compositions by formally trained musicians who use Western media to express traditional music, implying a pedagogical lineage through conservatories/ABC and a compositional mindset. Yoruba Art Music festivals foreground such formally composed works and the Westernized education that “colored” genres in classrooms and society. <cite id="09e42c59-0">In Nigeria, art music is the composition of Nigerians with formal music training who compose using Western media to express traditional music, with proposals for school-level art music instruction</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-1">Western formal education in Nigeria produced “colorations” in genres; the Yoruba Art Music festival showcases what constitutes art music through stage production of Yoruba works</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-3">The YAM festival emerged from debates on what constitutes art music, drawing on conventional traits and regional identities in the context of Western formal training</cite>.

- Repertoire circulation, venues, and audiences: Historiography notes that while popular music “travels in and out of the city,” art music localizes in a “cosmopolitan sphere,” reflecting elite institutions (symphonies, conservatories) and specialized reception. Ghana’s National Symphony Orchestra records highlife—a historically popular/vernacular classic—precisely to blur the high/low divide and reposition itself within Ghanaian cultural prestige, illustrating how institutions negotiate identity across categories. <cite id="a051c40c-0">Art music is least prominent; popular music is mobile, while art music is “locked in the cosmopolitan sphere”; the GNSO’s highlife recordings strategically blur elite (high art) and Ghanaian classic status as a status-elevation project</cite>.

- Transmission and documentation: Ethnomusicological practice documents and transcribes art-music repertoires using staff notation and analytic schemas, contrasting with ethnographic accounts of ritual/vernacular performance. In Central Cameroon, fieldwork explicitly employs Western staff notation with time signatures aligned to dance cycles, reflecting the analytical-literate orientation of art-music studies and performance practice, while acknowledging local tuning practices; related studies of lamellophones show school-based, secular pedagogy and overlap with sacred traditions, highlighting institutionalization versus ritual transmission. <cite id="b4e156bd-1">Fieldwork in central Cameroon uses Western staff notation and time signatures to capture performance structures, with tuning tuned to D major in many ensembles</cite> <cite id="b4e156bd-3">School-based karimba pedagogy and blending with Kwanongoma mbira illustrate institutionalized, secular practices that intermingle with sacred traditions, underscoring shifting boundaries</cite> <cite id="b4e156bd-0">Ethnomusicological canonization (e.g., mbira) and divergence from ritual origins show how performance contexts and scholarship shape genre status</cite>.

Case studies: Regional illustrations
- Nigeria (Yoruba and national discourse): YAM festival articulations and Nigerian analyses emphasize that Western formal education seeded “art music,” while contemporary Nigerian art music often blends indigenous materials with Western structures—evidence of hybridity within a formally trained, concert-oriented frame. Nigerian scholarship defines art music by formal training and Western compositional media; church and choral repertoire likewise synthesize Yoruba intonational contours with European harmonic frameworks to create contemporary art/church styles. <cite id="09e42c59-0">Nigerian art music is composed by formally trained musicians using Western media to express traditional music</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-1">Western formal education underpins genre colorations; YAM festival foregrounds art-music criteria through staged Yoruba works</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-4">Yoruba church music adapts pentatonic melodies to European-conceived diatonic chords, forming a stylistic paradigm for Nigerian contemporary art and church music</cite>.

- South Africa: Curricular analyses document Western classical “art music’s” dominance over Indigenous forms in South African music schools, producing marginalization and imbalances that decolonial scholarship seeks to redress; this institutional hierarchy mirrors the broader historiographical distinction between concert/classical infrastructure and oral/indigenous practices. <cite id="a051c40c-2">South African music schools prioritize Western classical “art music,” marginalizing local traditions; scholars call for integrating Indigenous music to decolonize curricula</cite>.

Hybridity, legitimacy, and critique
Scholarly historiography increasingly treats “art music” not as an anti-hybrid repository but as a space where African idioms are recombined with Western techniques. “Creative ethnomusicology” and neoclassical synthesis draw on indigenous elements to create concert works that claim both authenticity and innovation, while postcolonial theorists press for African ownership of theory and pedagogy. These currents complicate binary separations: African art music often foregrounds African sources, yet relies on Western compositional frameworks and institutions; conversely, popular/vernacular idioms gain reverence and enter concert discourse, blurring boundaries. <cite id="09e42c59-1">Nigerian art music scholarship situates Western art-music knowledge as a tool for conceptualizing indigenous practices, projecting African identity through art composition</cite> <cite id="09e42c59-2">Contemporary art composers blend African idioms with Western structures, using open-minded creative ethnomusicology to build a platform for cultural reclamation and modern expression</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Integration of traditional influences is common; vernacular idioms receive the same reverence as traditional sources in contemporary compositions</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-4">Kidula urges African-oriented theoretical tools and critiques the academy’s privileging of Western paradigms and oral-centric definitions, challenging how African music is valued</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-0">Institutions deliberately blur high/low to align with African cultural milieus, showing hybridity in repertoire and identity negotiation</cite>.

Cultural-function contrasts
Function and context remain central axes of distinction. Art music is typically framed as a contemplative, elite, and cosmopolitan practice centered on composed, notated, and rehearsed concert presentation, whereas popular/vernacular genres are mobile, embedded in everyday and market circuits, and often perform social, political, and ritual roles. Yet these are tendencies, not rigid laws: popular classics can be canonized and adopted by concert ensembles, and art-music ensembles can adopt vernacular repertoire to assert local prestige. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Art music combines expressive intent with high craftsmanship for concert presentation, while vernacular idioms are increasingly integrated by composers</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-0">Popular music travels beyond urban cores, whereas art music localizes in cosmopolitan spheres; Ghana’s NSO uses highlife to blur categories and elevate status</cite>.

Transmission and legitimation
Transmission patterns and legitimation strategies differentiate art music. Conservatory/ABC training, staff-notation literacy, and compositional authorship underwrite claims to craft and originality; oral apprenticeship and ritual transmission remain foundational for many traditions, though not exclusive to them. Scholarship documents how African musicians creatively appropriate notations to capture complex systems, and how institutions deploy analytic frameworks to legitimize new concert idioms. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-3">Staff and tonic solfa are widely used and cannot be dismissed as inauthentic despite foreign origins, as musicians rethink terms to fit African tone systems</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-0">Alternative transcription methods (e.g., Tonic Solfa; choral tonic solfa) address African rhythmic-melodic complexities, and competitions/festivals promote mass access to Western-educated composers</cite>.

What, then, distinguishes African art music in scholarly historiography?
- A concert-idiom orientation: designed for intent listening in concert settings, with aesthetic criteria emphasizing craft and structural coherence. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Art music is for concert presentation, combining expressive feeling with high craftsmanship and beauty</cite>.
- Western technique and notation as infrastructures: widespread use of staff/tonic solfa, conservatory/ABC training, and compositional methods adapted from Western art music, often alongside creative syncretism with African sources. <cite id="09e42c59-0">Nigerian art music is composed by formally trained musicians using Western media to express traditional music</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-3">Staff notation and tonic solfa are widely used and legitimized despite foreign origins; African specifics prompt rethinking of Western terminology</cite>.
- Institutional embedding: conservatories, symphonies, and festival stages, contrasted with the market- and community-driven circuits of popular/vernacular genres, though these boundaries blur. <cite id="a051c40c-0">Art music is least prominent and cosmopolitan; popular music is mobile; institutional repertoire choices (e.g., highlife) negotiate prestige and identity</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-2">Western classical “art music” dominates curricula in South Africa, marginalizing Indigenous forms in formal education</cite>.
- Analytic legitimation: acceptance into musicological analysis using the same parameters (melody, harmony, rhythm, form) that study Western art music, with transcriptions and examples in staff notation serving as markers of academic discourse. <cite id="472408a0-1">Scholarly legitimation demands structural analysis to grant African music legitimacy as musicology</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-3">Agawu insists African music be assessed with Western art-music paradigms, using staff notation as evidence of widely adopted representational systems</cite> <cite id="b4e156bd-1">Staff-notated transcriptions with time signatures document central Cameroonian performance structures</cite>.
- Hybridity and cultural reclamation: African art music often foregrounds indigenous idioms within Western frames; popular/vernacular elements enter concert discourse, complicating categorical separation. <cite id="09e42c59-2">Compositions integrate indigenous idioms with Western structures, serving as platforms for cultural reclamation and modern expression</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Vernacular idioms are treated with the same reverence as traditional sources in contemporary works</cite>.

Caveats and movements
Scholars caution that “art music” is a historically contingent category shaped by colonial education, missionary and missionary-linked church music, and postcolonial nation-building, and that essentializing binaries obscure fluid practices. Decolonial and ethnomusicological projects emphasize local knowledge production, oral traditions, and community-based pedagogies, urging inclusion of indigenous systems and cosmologies alongside Western ones. Within this flux, the historiographical distinction persists as a useful but negotiable frame: African art music is typically distinguished by its concert-intent, formal training, and Western-inflected compositionality, while other African musical traditions are rooted in ritual, everyday life, and popular markets; yet hybrid genres, church-music fusions, and institutional appropriations continually blur these lines. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-4">The academy privileges Euro-American paradigms; decolonial scholarship calls for African-oriented theories and methods</cite> <cite id="b4e156bd-0">Ethnomusicology’s canonization and divergent trajectories of mbira demonstrate how field attention and institutions shape genre status</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-4">Yoruba church music synthesizes African intonational contours with European harmony to form contemporary art/church styles</cite>.

In sum, scholarly historiography distinguishes African art music by its concert-centered aesthetics and craft, Western technique/notation infrastructures, formal conservatory training, institutional venues and audiences, and acceptance into musicological analysis, while recognizing that hybridity and decolonial critiques continually renegotiate these boundaries with other African musical traditions. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Art music combines expressive intent and craftsmanship for concert contexts</cite> <cite id="09e42c59-0">Nigerian art music is defined by formal training and Western media</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-3">Staff/tonic solfa and Western analytic frameworks are widely adopted and legitimized</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-0">Art music localizes in cosmopolitan spheres, while popular music travels; institutions strategically blur lines</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-2">Curricula privilege Western classical “art music,” prompting decolonial calls for inclusion of Indigenous forms</cite>.

Snippet: The study of African music traditionally falls under the academic discipline of ethnomusicology, but with this categorisation comes a degree of colonial baggage. Under the purview of ethnomusicology, many have approached the topic from sociological and/or anthropological perspectives, rather than musicological per se. While not without value, these approaches have tended to imbue African music with mysticism rather than engage with the music analytically. In this context has arisen an anti-formalist position, which suggests that it is inappropriate to analyse African music, because to do so is to impose an external world view on the subject. As has been powerfully argued, however, those who take this position simultaneously practise and apply other disciplinary formalisms to the subject, which opens up a raft of further questions and issues regarding the study of the cultural ‘other’. Recent developments in the musical academy have questioned the dichotomy of musicological and ethnomusicological practices. Further, a body of African scholars, led by Kofi Agawu, is recasting African music as a musicological rather than ethnomusicological topic. This approach calls for scholars to value, demand and practise greater structural analysis therein: to deny African music the right to analysis, some argue, is to deny it the right to legitimacy. This article discusses some of the key positions and practices in the historical study of African music, recent developments in detail, and projected futures for the discipline. Title: CONTINENTAL MUSICOLOGY: DECOLONISING THE MYTH OF A SINGULAR “AFRICAN MUSIC”
Snippet: When we turn to the rest of Africa, we find African societies whose musical cultures not only have their historical roots in the soil of Africa, but which also form a network of distinct yet related traditions which overlap in certain aspects of style, practice, or usage, and share common features of internal pattern, basic procedure, and contextual similarities. These related musical traditions constitute a family distinct from those of the West or the Orient in their areas of emphasis (ibid.: 4). 

Nketia reinforces the West-Orient-Africa trichotomy by stressing the distinctiveness of sub-Saharan Africa. This vision is shared, too, by Kubik whose conception of "African music" excludes the practices of "Arab-speaking North Africa" because of it "belonging to a Euro-Asian rather than African culture world. For similar reasons the music of European settler communities particularly in southern Africa, is not included" (Kubik 1994: 9). Kubik emphasizes that Khoisan and "pygmy" cultures are in fact quite different from those of their Bantu-speaking neighbours (1994: 13). In Nketia and Kubik's accounts of "African music, " then, distinctions between culture-areas are based at least in part on ethnicity. But they also rely on close description and analyses of specific musical practices, and efforts to extract shared principles from these practices. 

Blacking took a different view. He recognized context as essential to understanding "humanly organized sound" (1967: 5). There are many "musical traditions, " he wrote, "in which systems of sound organization are entirely artificial products of culture" (ibid.: 6). The emphasis on a socially constructed reality was indicative of a generation of music ethnographers who would emphasize a relativist understanding of music in and as culture (Titon 2009). Blacking's later work gestured toward the universalising tendencies of generative thinking while stressing the specifics of cultural manifestations. The reflexive paradigm that emerged in ethnomusicology of the 1980s and 1990s addressed questions of difference and representation (Kisliuk 1998) in the midst of the postcolonial moment. Identity politics were foregrounded in ethnographic studies conducted in situ.

Anthropology became the defining standard for studying African music, offering methodologies and theories that emphasised cultural context, social dynamics, and ethnographic fieldwork, which were seen as essential for capturing the broader meanings and functions of music within African societies. 34 Thus, while these scholars often approached their research with a love for music, it was within the disciplinary confines and methodologies of anthropology that they formalised their scholarly investigations into African musical traditions. 

From its inception, the study of ethnomusicology in the late 1800s, as the study of music from diverse cultures entered academia in Europe and America under the discipline comparative musicology, yielded two distinct approaches among scholars. 35 One approach favoured studying music as a standalone art form, focusing on its aesthetic qualities, technical aspects, and intrinsic musical characteristics. This perspective tended to prioritise music's formal properties and its theoretical frameworks, often detached from its social and cultural contexts. In contrast, the other approach emphasised studying music as a manifestation deeply embedded within the social structures and cultural practices of the communities where it originated. 36 Scholars adopting the latter approach sought to understand how music functioned within its societal context, examining its roles in rituals, ceremonies, social interactions, and cultural identity formation. This methodological stance viewed music as inseparable from the broader cultural fabric and social dynamics of the communities under study. These contrasting approaches, shaped by Euro-American scholars, became foundational methodologies in the study of African music and other global musical traditions. They reflect differing priorities in research, with one focusing on the intrinsic qualities of music itself and the other exploring how music reflects and shapes social realities within diverse cultural contexts. This distinction meant that Euro-American scholars, in their approaches to studying African music, did not prioritise the study of individual instruments or composers in the same way Western classical music centred on the compositions of great composers. 37

Title: Contemporary Ideas in African Art Music Composition: An Exploration of the Vocal and Instrumental Works of Seun Owoaje
Snippet: African art music continues to evolve through the contributions of contemporary composers who build on the legacies of their progenitors. Despite its growth, there has been a gap in the literature regarding its contemporary appeal, especially with respect to the works of modern African art music composers. Anchored on postcolonial theory, this study investigates the contemporary ideas shaping African art music composition by exploring the works of Seun Owoaje, a Nigerian composer known for his innovative integration of African musical idioms with Western structures. It aims to identify stylistic elements, thematic concerns, and compositional techniques employed by Seun Owoaje in his vocal and instrumental works. Adopting a qualitative design, data were sourced through in-depth oral interviews with the composer, coupled with analysis of his selected compositions. Seun Owoaje's music is informed by open-mindedness, creative ethnomusicology, social commentary, and inspiration from non-musical experiences. His works exhibit a deliberate blending of diverse musical traditions, reflect Yoruba cultural values, and offer philosophical insight on contemporary social issues through music commentary. The study contributes to the understanding of African art music as a platform for cultural reclamation and modern artistic expression, while providing valuable insights to teachers of music composition regarding blending innovative thinking with musical devices in the training of African art music composers. Research-based compositions should also be encouraged to blend indigenous elements with formal music training to ensure authenticity and innovation.

Snippet: The second rhetorical move that Agawu makes is built into the very structure of the book, and is treatise-like. In a sense this move is not new in that it elaborates arguments propounded in his earlier books, African Rhythm: A Northern Ewe Perspective (1995a) and Representing African Music (2003). The difference is that in The African Imagination in Music (2016) there is now a more systematic and encompassing approach to the problem, and he demands that "African music" be understood and appreciated using the self-same theoretical regimes as western art music. On the face of it, The African Imagination in Music offers an accessible introduction to African music; but it is also a treatise whose ambition is to show by rational means how the complexities of African music are readily intelligible in terms of the same paradigms and parameters used to study western art music. In fact, African music is fitted to the parameters of music theory, not vice versa. The structure of the book points to this determination with its chapter by chapter review of topics that include, inter alia, melody, harmony, rhythm, and form. Agawu contends that the "deep structures" of African music are reducible to the same structural hierarchies and terminologies as western music; it is the framing that is universal. Agawu is well aware of the strengths and weaknesses of this approach. He points out in his chapter on harmony, for instance, that western terminologies sometimes fail to account for the specifics of African tone systems; and he finds innovative ways in which to rethink these terms, or borrows new ones. But the rationale is always the same: to bring African musics into a western epistemic frame. 

This effort is made concrete in Agawu's use of staff notation, and, in a more substantial way, in his application of theory. "Surely, " he says, "both staff notation and tonic solfa are so widely used by literate or semi-literate African musicians that, despite their manifestly 'foreign' origins, they can no longer be dismissed as inauthentic ways of representing musical relations" (1995: 186).

Overview: Categories and their contested status
Historiography in African music studies has long grappled with how to classify “music” across cultural contexts. Early work often framed African music through anthropological or ethnomusicological lenses that emphasized cultural totality and performance-in-context, creating tensions with musicological approaches focused on formal analysis and concert practice. Over the twentieth century, scholars such as Kwabena Nketia helped found an African musicology that claimed structural analysis and legitimacy for African music within musicological discourse, while critiques highlighted that the academy has frequently represented African music through Euro-American paradigms and that “oralism” has been used to place African traditions in a lower epistemic position. These debates set the stage for distinguishing “art music” as a concert-oriented, formally trained, and analyzable tradition, contrasted with vernacular, ritual, and popular idioms, while also cautioning against essentializing categories. <cite id="472408a0-1">Recent developments question the musicological/ethnomusicological dichotomy and argue for structural analysis of African music as a legitimate object of musicology, countering anti-formalist critiques that deny analytic legitimacy to African music</cite> <cite id="472408a0-2">Nketia and Kubik delineate a “African music” distinct from West and Orient, emphasizing shared internal patterns and contextual similarities, while also grounding distinctions in ethnographic analysis and ethnicity</cite> <cite id="472408a0-4">African musicology emerges from Nketia’s program and ILAM, positioning African musicology as a distinct mode from ethnomusicology</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-4">Decolonial critiques argue African music remains framed by Euro-American theories and oral-centric definitions, prompting calls for African-oriented theoretical and methodological tools</cite>.

Operational distinctions in historiography
Scholarly treatments converge on several operational distinctions that mark “art music” in African historiography: concert-intent and aesthetics; Western techniques and notation; institutionalized training; repertoire circulation; and audience/space.

- Concert-intent, craftsmanship, and aesthetics: Historiography commonly defines art music as music designed for “intent listening” or concert presentation, combining expressive feeling with a high level of craftsmanship and sense of beauty; when African works are described as “art music,” they are understood as manifesting these attributes and being rooted in African traditions. This definition provides an evaluative but culturally relativized template for distinguishing concert repertoire from other genres. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Art music is defined as music for “concert” presentation combining expressive intent with high craftsmanship and beauty; African art music refers to works that manifest these attributes and are rooted in African traditions</cite>.

- Western techniques and notation as infrastructures: Comparative-historic work emphasizes how Western compositional techniques and notational systems (staff and tonic solfa) became central to African “art” composition, despite indigenous complexities. Agawu’s program argues African musics can be analyzed with the same theoretical regimes used for Western art music, insisting that widely adopted staff and tonic solfa notations, though “foreign,” no longer be dismissed as inauthentic because of their entrenched use by literate and semi-literate musicians. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Nigerian and Ghanaian studies show African composers integrating Western techniques and diverse idioms, treating vernacular influences with reverence as they adopt Western practices</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-3">Agawu contends African music can be fitted to Western parameters and argues staff notation and tonic solfa, despite foreign origins, are widely used and cannot be dismissed as inauthentic</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-0">Choral practice and competition/festival contexts have promoted transcription methods (e.g., Tonic Solfa) and show Western-educated African composers reaching mass audiences, underscoring the role of written systems</cite>.

- Formal conservatory/ABC pedagogy vs oral apprenticeship: Nigerian scholarship explicitly distinguishes “art music” as compositions by formally trained musicians who use Western media to express traditional music, implying a pedagogical lineage through conservatories/ABC and a compositional mindset. - Repertoire circulation, venues, and audiences: Historiography notes that while popular music “travels in and out of the city,” art music localizes in a “cosmopolitan sphere,” reflecting elite institutions (symphonies, conservatories) and specialized reception. Ghana’s National Symphony Orchestra records highlife—a historically popular/vernacular classic—precisely to blur the high/low divide and reposition itself within Ghanaian cultural prestige, illustrating how institutions negotiate identity across categories. <cite id="a051c40c-0">Art music is least prominent; popular music is mobile, while art music is “locked in the cosmopolitan sphere”; the GNSO’s highlife recordings strategically blur elite (high art) and Ghanaian classic status as a status-elevation project</cite>.

- Transmission and documentation: Ethnomusicological practice documents and transcribes art-music repertoires using staff notation and analytic schemas, contrasting with ethnographic accounts of ritual/vernacular performance. In Central Cameroon, fieldwork explicitly employs Western staff notation with time signatures aligned to dance cycles, reflecting the analytical-literate orientation of art-music studies and performance practice, while acknowledging local tuning practices; related studies of lamellophones show school-based, secular pedagogy and overlap with sacred traditions, highlighting institutionalization versus ritual transmission. <cite id="b4e156bd-1">Fieldwork in central Cameroon uses Western staff notation and time signatures to capture performance structures, with tuning tuned to D major in many ensembles</cite> <cite id="b4e156bd-3">School-based karimba pedagogy and blending with Kwanongoma mbira illustrate institutionalized, secular practices that intermingle with sacred traditions, underscoring shifting boundaries</cite> <cite id="b4e156bd-0">Ethnomusicological canonization (e.g., mbira) and divergence from ritual origins show how performance contexts and scholarship shape genre status</cite>.

Case studies: Regional illustrations
- Nigeria (Yoruba and national discourse): YAM festival articulations and Nigerian analyses emphasize that Western formal education seeded “art music,” while contemporary Nigerian art music often blends indigenous materials with Western structures—evidence of hybridity within a formally trained, concert-oriented frame. - Ghana: Institutional practice and historiography show art music’s elite orbit and relative scarcity compared to popular genres; Ghana’s National Symphony Orchestra records highlife to negotiate prestige within African cultural milieus, exemplifying the permeability of boundaries and the strategic use of “classical” status to legitimize reception by cosmopolitan audiences. <cite id="a051c40c-0">Art music remains least prominent; popular music’s mobility contrasts with art music’s cosmopolitan sphere; the GNSO’s highlife album blurs high/low as status elevation</cite>.

- South Africa: Curricular analyses document Western classical “art music’s” dominance over Indigenous forms in South African music schools, producing marginalization and imbalances that decolonial scholarship seeks to redress; this institutional hierarchy mirrors the broader historiographical distinction between concert/classical infrastructure and oral/indigenous practices. <cite id="a051c40c-2">South African music schools prioritize Western classical “art music,” marginalizing local traditions; scholars call for integrating Indigenous music to decolonize curricula</cite>.

Hybridity, legitimacy, and critique
Scholarly historiography increasingly treats “art music” not as an anti-hybrid repository but as a space where African idioms are recombined with Western techniques. “Creative ethnomusicology” and neoclassical synthesis draw on indigenous elements to create concert works that claim both authenticity and innovation, while postcolonial theorists press for African ownership of theory and pedagogy. These currents complicate binary separations: African art music often foregrounds African sources, yet relies on Western compositional frameworks and institutions; conversely, popular/vernacular idioms gain reverence and enter concert discourse, blurring boundaries. <cite id="09e42c59-1">Nigerian art music scholarship situates Western art-music knowledge as a tool for conceptualizing indigenous practices, projecting African identity through art composition</cite> <cite id="09e42c59-2">Contemporary art composers blend African idioms with Western structures, using open-minded creative ethnomusicology to build a platform for cultural reclamation and modern expression</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Integration of traditional influences is common; vernacular idioms receive the same reverence as traditional sources in contemporary compositions</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-4">Kidula urges African-oriented theoretical tools and critiques the academy’s privileging of Western paradigms and oral-centric definitions, challenging how African music is valued</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-0">Institutions deliberately blur high/low to align with African cultural milieus, showing hybridity in repertoire and identity negotiation</cite>.

Cultural-function contrasts
Function and context remain central axes of distinction. Art music is typically framed as a contemplative, elite, and cosmopolitan practice centered on composed, notated, and rehearsed concert presentation, whereas popular/vernacular genres are mobile, embedded in everyday and market circuits, and often perform social, political, and ritual roles. Yet these are tendencies, not rigid laws: popular classics can be canonized and adopted by concert ensembles, and art-music ensembles can adopt vernacular repertoire to assert local prestige. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Art music combines expressive intent with high craftsmanship for concert presentation, while vernacular idioms are increasingly integrated by composers</cite> <cite id="a051c40c-0">Popular music travels beyond urban cores, whereas art music localizes in cosmopolitan spheres; Ghana’s NSO uses highlife to blur categories and elevate status</cite>.

Transmission and legitimation
Transmission patterns and legitimation strategies differentiate art music. Conservatory/ABC training, staff-notation literacy, and compositional authorship underwrite claims to craft and originality; oral apprenticeship and ritual transmission remain foundational for many traditions, though not exclusive to them. Scholarship documents how African musicians creatively appropriate notations to capture complex systems, and how institutions deploy analytic frameworks to legitimize new concert idioms. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-3">Staff and tonic solfa are widely used and cannot be dismissed as inauthentic despite foreign origins, as musicians rethink terms to fit African tone systems</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-0">Alternative transcription methods (e.g., Tonic Solfa; choral tonic solfa) address African rhythmic-melodic complexities, and competitions/festivals promote mass access to Western-educated composers</cite>.

- A concert-idiom orientation: designed for intent listening in concert settings, with aesthetic criteria emphasizing craft and structural coherence. <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Art music is for concert presentation, combining expressive feeling with high craftsmanship and beauty</cite>.

- Hybridity and cultural reclamation: African art music often foregrounds indigenous idioms within Western frames; popular/vernacular elements enter concert discourse, complicating categorical separation. <cite id="09e42c59-2">Compositions integrate indigenous idioms with Western structures, serving as platforms for cultural reclamation and modern expression</cite> <cite id="a6ac9eb1-1">Vernacular idioms are treated with the same reverence as traditional sources in contemporary works</cite>.

Caveats and movements
Scholars caution that “art music” is a historically contingent category shaped by colonial education, missionary and missionary-linked church music, and postcolonial nation-building, and that essentializing binaries obscure fluid practices. Decolonial and ethnomusicological projects emphasize local knowledge production, oral traditions, and community-based pedagogies, urging inclusion of indigenous systems and cosmologies alongside Western ones. Title: CONTINENTAL MUSICOLOGY: DECOLONISING THE MYTH OF A SINGULAR “AFRICAN MUSIC”
Snippet: When we turn to the rest of Africa, we find African societies whose musical cultures not only have their historical roots in the soil of Africa, but which also form a network of distinct yet related traditions which overlap in certain aspects of style, practice, or usage, and share common features of internal pattern, basic procedure, and contextual similarities. These related musical traditions constitute a family distinct from those of the West or the Orient in their areas of emphasis (ibid.: 4). 

Nketia reinforces the West-Orient-Africa trichotomy by stressing the distinctiveness of sub-Saharan Africa. This vision is shared, too, by Kubik whose conception of "African music" excludes the practices of "Arab-speaking North Africa" because of it "belonging to a Euro-Asian rather than African culture world. For similar reasons the music of European settler communities particularly in southern Africa, is not included" (Kubik 1994: 9). Kubik emphasizes that Khoisan and "pygmy" cultures are in fact quite different from those of their Bantu-speaking neighbours (1994: 13). In Nketia and Kubik's accounts of "African music, " then, distinctions between culture-areas are based at least in part on ethnicity. But they also rely on close description and analyses of specific musical practices, and efforts to extract shared principles from these practices. 

Blacking took a different view. He recognized context as essential to understanding "humanly organized sound" (1967: 5). There are many "musical traditions, " he wrote, "in which systems of sound organization are entirely artificial products of culture" (ibid.: 6). The emphasis on a socially constructed reality was indicative of a generation of music ethnographers who would emphasize a relativist understanding of music in and as culture (Titon 2009). Blacking's later work gestured toward the universalising tendencies of generative thinking while stressing the specifics of cultural manifestations. The reflexive paradigm that emerged in ethnomusicology of the 1980s and 1990s addressed questions of difference and representation (Kisliuk 1998) in the midst of the postcolonial moment. Identity politics were foregrounded in ethnographic studies conducted in situ.
